Banana-healthy-leaf.cause: No pathogen detected — the leaf shows the uniform green colour and intact tissue of a well-nourished plant.
Banana-healthy-leaf.symptoms: Even green colour, no lesions, streaks, wilting or discoloration along the veins.
Banana-healthy-leaf.treatment: No action needed. Keep up good spacing, drainage and regular field checks so problems are caught early.

Banana-black-sigatoka.cause: A fungus (Mycosphaerella fijiensis) that spreads through wind-blown spores and thrives in humid conditions, worsened by dense planting and poor drainage.
Banana-black-sigatoka.symptoms: Reddish-brown streaks on the leaf that darken into black necrotic blotches ringed with yellow, eventually killing large patches of leaf tissue.
Banana-black-sigatoka.treatment: Cut off and destroy heavily infected leaves, improve drainage and plant spacing for airflow, apply a recommended fungicide (e.g. mancozeb or propiconazole) following local agricultural extension guidance, and favour tolerant banana varieties where possible.

Banana-fusarium-wilt.cause: A soil-borne fungus (Fusarium oxysporum f.sp. cubense) that enters through the roots and can persist in soil for decades; it spreads via infected suckers, tools and irrigation water.
Banana-fusarium-wilt.symptoms: Yellowing that starts at the margins of older leaves, leaves wilting and collapsing around the stem, and brown-black streaking inside the pseudostem when cut.
Banana-fusarium-wilt.treatment: There is no cure once a plant is infected — uproot and destroy affected plants, avoid replanting bananas in the same soil, use certified disease-free (tissue-culture) planting material, disinfect tools between plants, and plant resistant cultivars where available.

Bean-healthy-leaf.cause: No pathogen detected — the leaf shows normal colour and structure.
Bean-healthy-leaf.symptoms: Uniform green leaf, no dark lesions, pustules or angular spots.
Bean-healthy-leaf.treatment: No action needed. Continue crop rotation and regular scouting to catch any issues early.

Bean-anthra-leaf.cause: A fungus (Colletotrichum lindemuthianum) spread by infected seed, splashing rain and contaminated tools or hands, especially in cool, wet conditions.
Bean-anthra-leaf.symptoms: Dark, sunken lesions on pods and stems, with angular brown-to-black spots along the leaf veins, most visible on the underside of the leaf.
Bean-anthra-leaf.treatment: Plant certified disease-free seed, rotate out of beans for 2-3 years, remove and burn crop debris after harvest, avoid working the field while leaves are wet, and apply an approved fungicide if the infection is severe.

Bean-rust-leaf.cause: A fungus (Uromyces appendiculatus) spread by wind-borne spores, favoured by warm, humid weather and a dense leaf canopy.
Bean-rust-leaf.symptoms: Small reddish-brown raised pustules on the underside of leaves, each surrounded by a yellow halo; heavy infection causes early leaf drop.
Bean-rust-leaf.treatment: Plant resistant varieties, space plants for good airflow, remove volunteer bean plants and old crop debris, and apply fungicide at the first sign of infection if pressure is heavy.

Maize-healthy-leaf.cause: No pathogen detected — normal leaf colour and structure.
Maize-healthy-leaf.symptoms: Uniform green blade, no streaking, mottling or necrosis.
Maize-healthy-leaf.treatment: No action needed. Keep monitoring for insect vectors that can introduce viral disease later in the season.

Maize-lethal-necrosis.cause: A viral disease caused by co-infection with Maize Chlorotic Mottle Virus and a cereal potyvirus, transmitted by thrips, aphids and beetles, and sometimes carried in seed.
Maize-lethal-necrosis.symptoms: Chlorotic mottling starting near the leaf base, progressing to yellowing and dead (necrotic) tissue spreading out from the midrib, stunted plants and poor or absent cob formation.
Maize-lethal-necrosis.treatment: There is no chemical cure — uproot and destroy infected plants early, control the insect vectors, plant certified virus-free seed, rotate with non-cereal crops, and avoid planting maize continuously in the same field.

Maize-streak-virus.cause: A virus transmitted by leafhoppers, which spreads quickly in warm weather, especially where volunteer maize or grassy weeds host the insect vector nearby.
Maize-streak-virus.symptoms: Narrow, pale yellow or white broken streaks running parallel to the leaf veins, stunted growth and smaller cobs.
Maize-streak-virus.treatment: Control leafhopper vectors with insecticide or intercropping, plant resistant or tolerant varieties, remove volunteer maize and grassy weeds around the field, and plant early to avoid the peak vector season.
